name: Share of the serviceable market that buys a dedicated launch
question: Q1
rationale: Revealed preference: the share of the serviceable market that bought a dedicated small-launcher ride instead of rideshare (view v_penetration_evidence, GCAT). In Andøya's band 2024 and 2025 together: 7.0 % of mass and 9.3 % of satellites (2024: 12.8 % / 15.1 %, 2025: 4.2 % / 6.7 %); Western open market, all orbits: 8.4 % of mass, 9.1 % of satellites. BryceTech: 17–23 % of non-broadband smallsats worldwide 2023–2025, but including Chinese small launchers. 7 % = the two-year mass share in Isar's band, the conservative end of these benchmarks. Range: 4 % (2025 mass share) to 15 % (2024 band share and the share not flown on Falcon 9, 13–18 %). How much of it Isar wins is the separate lever som_win_share. New rockets get demo payloads first (Planet)

name: Launch success rate
question: Q1
rationale: Insurance of about 25% on Isar's next mission implies 75%; mature launchers reach 92–95%

name: Isar's share of the dedicated demand
question: Q1
rationale: Isar's share of the dedicated demand against Rocket Lab and later entrants (view v_win_share_evidence, GCAT). In Andøya's band in 2024 and 2025, European operators (Kinéis, OroraTech) bought 44 % of the dedicated mass (58 % of satellites), all on Electron because no European small launcher flew yet: Isar's natural share. Isar also signs non-European customers (Planet, Astroscale, ElevationSpace, SEOPS), but new rockets get demo payloads first (Planet). Base 45 %. Range: 20 % (demo phase; the second supplier, Firefly Alpha, took about a sixth of the band's dedicated satellites in 2024) to 100 % (the earlier implicit assumption, e.g. if Rocket Lab is not an option for a customer)
